titre: Grand Rapids, 1945: The Fluoridation Trial Cut Short by Its Own Success
accroche: On January 25, 1945, Grand Rapids fluoridates its water for the first time. The trial, planned to run fifteen years, stops after barely six.
contenu_vulgarise:
On January 25, 1945, at four in the afternoon, engineers at the Monroe Avenue Water Filtration Plant in Grand Rapids, Michigan, begin adding a controlled amount of sodium fluoride to the city's water. It is the first time a municipality voluntarily fluoridates its public water supply. The move answers an observation made by epidemiologist H. Trendley Dean, of the U.S. Public Health Service: in cities where the water naturally contains fluoride, children have markedly fewer cavities. What remains to be checked is whether adding fluoride artificially produces the same effect.

## A trial designed to run fifteen years

To find out, Grand Rapids is paired with Muskegon, a nearby city whose water stays fluoride-free: the control city. In 1944-1945, every child aged four to sixteen is examined in both cities, 28,614 in Grand Rapids and 7,786 in Muskegon, to establish a baseline dental record before any treatment. The protocol, run with the Michigan Department of Health and the University of Michigan School of Dentistry, is meant to follow both populations for fifteen years, long enough to watch an entire generation of children grow up with, or without, fluoride in their water from birth.

The first results, published in 1950, already show a sharp drop in cavities in Grand Rapids: a decline of about 60% from the initial baseline. A more detailed report on the trial's seventh year, by Francis Arnold, Trendley Dean and John Knutson, confirms the trend in 1953. This is where the trial takes an unplanned turn.

## Cut short by its own success

Muskegon's residents are watching their neighboring city's results too. In 1951, convinced by what they observe in Grand Rapids, the city's officials decide to fluoridate their own water supply. The move makes sense for a city that wants the same dental protection for its own children. It does, however, end, after six of the planned fifteen years, nine years earlier than scheduled, the existence of a true fluoride-free control city: from 1951 on, Grand Rapids has nothing left to compare itself to.

Follow-ups continue regardless through the fifteenth year, in 1962, and keep reporting sharp declines in children's cavities. But the control city's early loss weakened the rigor of those later figures: after 1951, it is no longer clear what the fluoridated water changed, compared to water that was, in any case, about to become fluoridated too.

The founding trial of water fluoridation, then, could never unfold as planned on paper. It did not fail: it convinced the city meant to serve as its point of comparison too quickly for the comparison to last. Other similar trials, run around the same time in other U.S. and Canadian cities, later helped confirm the effect without depending on this one pair of cities alone.

repere.texte: The water fluoridation trial launched in Grand Rapids in 1945 was meant to run fifteen years, with Muskegon serving as the fluoride-free control city. Convinced by the results observed in Grand Rapids, Muskegon's officials decided to fluoridate their own water in 1951, ending the study nine years early.
repere.source: Goin, Dana E. et al., “Water Fluoridation and Birth Outcomes in California,” Environmental Health Perspectives, vol. 132, no. 5, 2024, article 057004

carte.punch: The first water fluoridation trial never got to run as planned.
carte.idee: Launched in 1945 in Grand Rapids, with Muskegon as its fluoride-free control city, the trial was meant to last fifteen years. By 1950, cavities had already dropped about 60% in Grand Rapids. Convinced, Muskegon fluoridated its own water in 1951: the comparison ended nine years ahead of schedule.

quiz.question: Why did the Grand Rapids fluoridation trial, planned to run fifteen years, stop after only six?
choix: Because Muskegon, the control city, fluoridated its own water in 1951, convinced by the results observed in Grand Rapids
Because sodium fluoride turned out to be toxic and the experiment had to be stopped
Because the U.S. Public Health Service ran out of funding to continue the dental follow-up
Because Grand Rapids stopped fluoridating its water after residents complained
quiz.explication: By 1950, cavities among Grand Rapids children had already dropped sharply. Convinced by these results, Muskegon, which was meant to remain a fluoride-free control city for fifteen years, fluoridated its own water in 1951: the comparison stopped making sense nine years before it was due to end.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What observation was the hypothesis tested in Grand Rapids from 1945 based on?
choix: Fluoride speeds up tooth eruption in young children
Cities whose water naturally contains fluoride have fewer dental cavities
Residents who drink bottled water have more cavities
Fluoride lowers the risk of bone fractures in the elderly
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Epidemiologist H. Trendley Dean observed that cities whose water naturally contains fluoride have markedly fewer cavities, hence the idea of testing a controlled fluoride addition to Grand Rapids's water.

28,614 in Grand Rapids and 7,786 in Muskegon

quiz_supplementaire.explication: Every child aged four to sixteen was examined before any treatment, 28,614 in Grand Rapids and 7,786 in Muskegon, to establish a baseline dental record.

quiz_supplementaire.question: By how much had cavities among Grand Rapids children declined by 1950, compared with the baseline?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The first results, published in 1950, show a decline of about 60% in cavities among Grand Rapids children, compared with the baseline established in 1944-1945.
